summary: The article describes the emerging trend of ARG (Alternate Reality Game) pilgrimages, in which players travel the world to follow game narratives through real places. It profiles pioneers like Michael Robertson, Alexis Taylor and Jasmine Flores, and cites games such as The Continuum and The Dalriadan Codex. It also covers the communal nature of these journeys and their economic benefits for host cities like Edinburgh.
one_line: ARG pilgrimages are a new travel trend where players follow alternate reality game narratives across real-world locations, forming communities and boosting local economies.
key_facts: Alternate Reality Games (ARGs) are interactive, networked narratives that use the real world as a platform, often across multiple media, and can be affected by participants' ideas or actions.
September 12, 2023 is described as the historic moment when a small group of adventurers set out on the first of many 'alternative reality' sojourns.
Michael Robertson and Alexis Taylor, pioneers of ARG pilgrimages, first met in an online forum dedicated to ARGs.
Robertson and Taylor began their journey on October 1, 2023, leaving from different corners of the globe.
Pilgrimage sites span from Burning Man, where clues were woven into the festival, to the catacombs beneath Paris.
On November 15, 2023, a game called 'The Continuum' brought a wave of pilgrims to Machu Picchu, blending Inca history with a story of cosmic significance.
Each pilgrim carries an artifact, such as a strange coin, a tattered journal, or a digital key.
Jasmine Flores discovered a clue embedded in the soundscape of a Mumbai marketplace on December 5, 2023.
Jasmine Flores said: 'The ARG was a soundtrack to the dance of life around me.'
ARG pilgrimages are communal, with connections formed through forums, clue exchanges, and unplanned rendezvous, creating a festival-like atmosphere.
On January 22, 2024, Edinburgh's alleyways hosted The Dalriadan Codex, a Celtic-inspired narrative game.
Edinburgh's local economy surged as hotels, restaurants, and shops catered to players of The Dalriadan Codex.
The article says game-makers act like modern-day Griots, threading epics through screens, old letters, and strangers on park benches.
